prompt: A stack removes items in which order relative to how they were added?
optionA: Items are removed in sorted order
optionB: The last item added is removed first
optionC: Items are removed in a random order
optionD: The first item added is removed first
correctAnswerText: The last item added is removed first
explanation: A stack is last-in, first-out. The most recently pushed item is the one on top, and the top is the only item pop can reach. Removing the first item added is queue behaviour.

prompt: Which operation adds an item to a stack?
optionA: peek
optionB: push
optionC: pop
optionD: enqueue
correctAnswerText: push
explanation: push adds to the top. pop removes from the top, peek reads the top without removing, and enqueue belongs to a queue.

prompt: Which item does pop remove from a stack?
optionA: The item at the top
optionB: The item added first
optionC: The smallest item
optionD: The item at the bottom
correctAnswerText: The item at the top
explanation: pop only ever reaches the top. Nothing in a stack lets you remove from the bottom or search for a particular value — that restriction is the whole point of the structure.

prompt: What does peek do to a stack?
optionA: Returns every item in order
optionB: Returns the bottom item and leaves the stack unchanged
optionC: Returns the top item and removes it
optionD: Returns the top item and leaves the stack unchanged
correctAnswerText: Returns the top item and leaves the stack unchanged
explanation: peek reads without removing. Confusing it with pop is the commonest source of a stack that empties faster than the code intends.

prompt: What does isEmpty report about a stack?
optionA: Whether it has ever held an item
optionB: Whether it currently holds no items
optionC: Whether every item in it is zero
optionD: Whether it has reached its maximum size
correctAnswerText: Whether it currently holds no items
explanation: isEmpty is about the present count, not about capacity and not about history. A stack that has been filled and emptied again is empty.

prompt: Which items in a stack can be accessed directly?
optionA: Only the item on top
optionB: The top and the bottom item
optionC: Any item, by its position
optionD: Any item, by its value
correctAnswerText: Only the item on top
explanation: Only the top is reachable. Indexing into the middle is an array operation; a structure that allowed it would not be a stack.

prompt: Which everyday feature behaves like a stack?
optionA: A scheduled backup that runs nightly
optionB: A printer queue, which prints jobs in the order received
optionC: Undo, which reverses the most recent action first
optionD: A sorted contact list
correctAnswerText: Undo, which reverses the most recent action first
explanation: Undo reverses the most recent action first, which is last-in first-out. A printer queue is first-in first-out, and the other two involve no removal order at all.

prompt: What happens when pop is called on an empty stack?
optionA: It is an error condition the code must handle
optionB: It silently does nothing and is always safe
optionC: It returns the last item that was removed
optionD: It returns zero
correctAnswerText: It is an error condition the code must handle
explanation: There is nothing to return, so the operation cannot succeed. Most languages raise; the point is that the caller must check first rather than assume a value comes back.

prompt: The structure a language uses to track which function must be returned to is called:
optionA: The queue
optionB: The symbol table
optionC: The heap
optionD: The call stack
correctAnswerText: The call stack
explanation: Each call pushes a frame and each return pops one, which is why it is a stack. The heap holds allocated objects and has no such ordering.

prompt: Where does push place a new item?
optionA: At the bottom, below everything already there
optionB: Wherever there is free space
optionC: In sorted position among the existing items
optionD: On top, above everything already there
correctAnswerText: On top, above everything already there
explanation: push always adds on top, which is why the most recent item is the one pop reaches. Nothing about a stack sorts or searches for a position.

prompt: Starting from an empty stack: push 3, push 7, push 9. What does pop return?
optionC: Nothing — the stack is empty
explanation: 9 was pushed last, so it sits on top and pop reaches it first. Answering 3 is reading the structure as a queue.

prompt: Starting from an empty stack: push 4, push 8, pop, push 2. What is on top now?
optionB: The stack is empty
explanation: The pop removed 8, leaving 4. Pushing 2 then puts it above 4, so 2 is on top.

prompt: Starting from an empty stack: push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, push 4, pop. How many items remain?
explanation: Four pushes and two pops leave two items. Counting operations rather than tracking the net change is where this usually goes wrong.

prompt: The letters A, B, C are pushed in that order, then all three are popped. In what order do they come out?
optionA: B, C, A
optionB: A, C, B
optionC: A, B, C
optionD: C, B, A
correctAnswerText: C, B, A
explanation: Pushing then popping everything reverses the sequence, which is the property that makes a stack useful for reversal problems.

prompt: The same three values are added to a stack and to a queue, then all are removed from each. How do the two output orders relate?
optionA: The stack produces sorted output and the queue does not
optionB: The stack produces the reverse of the queue
optionC: The relationship depends on the values
optionD: They produce the same order
correctAnswerText: The stack produces the reverse of the queue
explanation: A queue preserves the insertion order and a stack reverses it, so one is the reverse of the other whatever the values are.

prompt: A stack holds three items. peek is called twice. How many items does it hold afterwards?
explanation: peek never removes, so calling it any number of times leaves the size unchanged. Expecting 1 treats peek as pop.

prompt: push 5, push 6, pop, push 7, pop, pop. What is the sequence of popped values?
explanation: The first pop takes 6, then 7 is pushed and immediately popped, and the last pop takes 5 — the only item left.

prompt: A browser back button returns to the most recently visited page first. Which structure does this behaviour match?
optionA: A queue
optionB: A sorted list
optionC: A hash map
optionD: A stack
correctAnswerText: A stack
explanation: Most-recent-first is last-in first-out. Each page visit pushes, and going back pops.

prompt: A stack starts empty. Equal numbers of pushes and pops are performed, and no pop is ever called on an empty stack. What is its final state?
optionA: Holding as many items as there were pushes
optionB: Empty
optionC: Holding one item
optionD: Impossible to determine without the values
correctAnswerText: Empty
explanation: Each push adds one and each pop removes one, so equal counts return the size to zero regardless of what the values were.

prompt: To find whether a particular value sits somewhere inside a stack, you must:
optionA: Pop items off until you find it, losing the ones removed unless you keep them
optionB: Call a built-in search that inspects every item without removing any
optionC: Use an index to jump straight to it
optionD: Sort the stack first, then search it
correctAnswerText: Pop items off until you find it, losing the ones removed unless you keep them
explanation: A stack exposes only the top, so reaching the middle means removing what is above. Needing to search is a strong sign a stack is the wrong structure.

prompt: When checking whether brackets in an expression are balanced, what does the algorithm do on meeting a closing bracket?
optionA: Pop the stack and check the popped opener matches this closer
optionB: Count the closers and compare the total with the openers
optionC: Push the closing bracket so it can be compared at the end
optionD: Search the stack for a matching opener wherever it sits
correctAnswerText: Pop the stack and check the popped opener matches this closer
explanation: The most recent unmatched opener is on top, which is exactly the one a closer must match. Counting alone accepts ")(" as balanced, which it is not.

prompt: A bracket-matching algorithm reaches the end of the input with nothing left unmatched so far. What final check is still required?
optionA: No further check is needed
optionB: That the last character was a closing bracket
optionC: That the stack is empty
optionD: That the input length was even
correctAnswerText: That the stack is empty
explanation: Anything left on the stack is an opener that was never closed, so "((" would otherwise pass. An even length proves nothing.

prompt: To reverse a sequence using a stack, what is the procedure?
optionA: Push and pop alternately as you go
optionB: Push every second item, then pop them all
optionC: Push every item, then read the stack from the bottom
optionD: Push every item in order, then pop them all
correctAnswerText: Push every item in order, then pop them all
explanation: Pushing preserves order going in and popping reverses it coming out. Reading from the bottom is not an operation a stack offers.

prompt: An editor supports both undo and redo. How is this usually built?
optionA: A sorted list ordered by timestamp
optionB: One queue, read from either end
optionC: Two stacks — undone actions move from one to the other
optionD: One stack, with a pointer moved up and down it
correctAnswerText: Two stacks — undone actions move from one to the other
explanation: Undoing pops from the undo stack and pushes onto the redo stack; a new action clears redo. Both halves need last-in first-out, so both are stacks.

prompt: A recursive function is rewritten as a loop. What usually has to be introduced?
optionA: Nothing — any recursion becomes a loop directly
optionB: An explicit stack holding what each pending call was going to do
optionC: A counter recording how many calls were made
optionD: A queue, to process the calls in the order they were made
correctAnswerText: An explicit stack holding what each pending call was going to do
explanation: Recursion uses the call stack implicitly; removing it means keeping that state yourself. Only simple tail recursion converts with no structure at all.

prompt: Which problem characteristic most strongly suggests a stack?
optionA: Items must be processed in the order they arrived
optionB: The most recently opened thing must be closed first
optionC: Items must be retrieved by a key
optionD: The largest item must be found quickly
correctAnswerText: The most recently opened thing must be closed first
explanation: Nesting — brackets, tags, function calls, scopes — is the shape a stack fits. Arrival order wants a queue, key lookup a map, and largest-first a heap.

prompt: Checking "([)]" with a bracket-matching stack, where does it fail?
optionA: At the end, because the stack still holds an unmatched opening bracket
optionB: At ")", because the top of the stack is "[" rather than "("
optionC: It does not fail — the counts balance
optionD: At "]", because the stack is empty by then
correctAnswerText: At ")", because the top of the stack is "[" rather than "("
explanation: The closer must match the most recent opener, which is "[". Interleaved brackets like this are exactly what counting alone cannot catch.

prompt: Implementing a stack on top of a dynamic array, which end should be the top?
optionA: Either end, because adding and removing cost the same wherever you do it
optionB: The end, because appending and removing there costs constant time
optionC: The middle, to keep both ends free
optionD: The start, because it is easier to find
correctAnswerText: The end, because appending and removing there costs constant time
explanation: Removing from the front shifts every remaining element, making each operation linear. Using the end keeps push and pop constant time.

prompt: Evaluating the postfix expression "3 4 + 2 *" with a stack, what happens on reading "+"?
optionA: The next value is popped and added to a running total
optionB: Two values are popped, added, and the result pushed back
optionC: Everything on the stack is summed
optionD: The "+" is pushed to be applied later
correctAnswerText: Two values are popped, added, and the result pushed back
explanation: An operator consumes its operands from the top and returns one value, which becomes an operand for whatever follows. Here 3 and 4 become 7, then 7 and 2 become 14.

prompt: What is the cost of push and pop on a well-implemented stack?
optionA: It depends on how many items the stack holds
optionB: Linear time, because the items must be shifted
optionC: Constant time, because only the top is touched
optionD: Logarithmic time, because the stack is kept balanced
correctAnswerText: Constant time, because only the top is touched
explanation: Neither operation looks past the top, so the size is irrelevant. That cheapness is much of why stacks are used where they fit.

prompt: A bracket checker pops on every closing bracket without first checking the stack. On which input does it fail?
optionA: "()" — the stack is emptied correctly
optionB: "(())" — the nesting is handled
optionC: It cannot fail; popping an empty stack is harmless
optionD: ")(" — the first character pops an empty stack
correctAnswerText: ")(" — the first character pops an empty stack
explanation: A closer arriving with nothing open is unbalanced input, and the code must report that rather than pop nothing. This is the case a checker written only against valid input always misses.

prompt: A loop meant to empty a stack calls peek instead of pop each time. What happens?
optionA: It processes each item exactly once and terminates
optionB: It terminates immediately without processing anything
optionC: It processes the items in reverse order
optionD: It never terminates, because the stack never shrinks
correctAnswerText: It never terminates, because the stack never shrinks
explanation: peek leaves the stack unchanged, so a loop conditioned on it being non-empty never reaches its exit. The symptom is a hang, not a wrong answer.

prompt: A bracket checker returns true as soon as the input ends, without examining the stack. Which input does it wrongly accept?
explanation: Three openers leave three items on the stack and no closer ever contradicts them. The closers-only case fails earlier, on the unguarded pop.

prompt: An undo feature removes the oldest action rather than the newest. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: The stack is being popped twice per undo
optionB: A queue is being used where a stack is needed
optionC: The stack has exceeded its capacity
optionD: The actions are being sorted before removal
correctAnswerText: A queue is being used where a stack is needed
explanation: Oldest-first is first-in first-out, which is queue behaviour. The symptom names the structure exactly.

prompt: A long-running program pushes onto a stack in a loop and pops only in a branch that rarely runs. What is the symptom?
optionA: Memory use grows steadily until the process runs out
optionB: The program slows but memory stays flat
optionC: The stack silently discards its oldest items
optionD: push begins to fail immediately
correctAnswerText: Memory use grows steadily until the process runs out
explanation: Nothing bounds a stack automatically, so unmatched pushes accumulate. The structure does not evict anything to make room.

prompt: A recursive function raises a stack overflow on a large input but works on a small one. What does that indicate?
optionA: The input contains a value the function cannot handle
optionB: The function allocates too much memory per call, exhausting the heap rather than the stack
optionC: The recursion has no base case at all
optionD: Each call adds a frame, and the depth exceeded what the call stack holds
correctAnswerText: Each call adds a frame, and the depth exceeded what the call stack holds
explanation: Working on small input rules out a missing base case — that would fail at every size. The depth itself is the problem, which is why an explicit stack or an iterative form fixes it.

prompt: Items are pushed onto a stack and then popped into a list, and the list comes out backwards. What is wrong?
optionA: The pushes happened in the wrong order, so the stack was built backwards
optionB: The list is being built from the end
optionC: The stack was not emptied fully
optionD: Nothing is wrong — that is what a stack does; the code wanted a queue
correctAnswerText: Nothing is wrong — that is what a stack does; the code wanted a queue
explanation: Reversal is the defining behaviour, not a defect. A program surprised by it has chosen the wrong structure for what it wanted.

prompt: A function searches a stack by popping until it finds a value, then returns. What has it done to the stack?
optionA: Left the stack exactly as it was
optionB: Discarded everything above the match, and the match itself
optionC: Reversed the order of everything that was left behind
optionD: Left only the matching item
correctAnswerText: Discarded everything above the match, and the match itself
explanation: Popped items are gone unless the code deliberately keeps them. A search that destroys what it searched is a bug hidden inside a function that appears to work.

prompt: Two parts of a program push and pop on the same stack instance. Occasionally one pops a value the other pushed. Why?
optionA: The stack has been sorted by one of the callers, moving items out of order
optionB: One caller is using peek rather than pop
optionC: A stack has no notion of ownership — the top belongs to whoever pops next
optionD: Stacks are not safe to read at all once shared
correctAnswerText: A stack has no notion of ownership — the top belongs to whoever pops next
explanation: The structure offers no way to reserve or tag items. Two independent users need two stacks, or a discipline the structure itself cannot enforce.

prompt: An array-backed stack keeps a "top" index. After pushing one item to an empty stack, top is 1 and reading at that index gives nothing. What is the likely error?
optionA: The item was pushed to the front rather than the end, so the index misses it
optionB: The array was not allocated with enough space
optionC: top is being incremented before the item is written, so it points past the item
optionD: top should always be zero for a one-item stack
correctAnswerText: top is being incremented before the item is written, so it points past the item
explanation: Whether top means "the last used slot" or "the next free slot" must be decided once and honoured by both push and pop. Mixing the two conventions is the classic off-by-one here.

prompt: A list only ever has items added and removed at one end, but the team uses an array with index access everywhere. What is the strongest argument for a stack instead?
optionA: It uses measurably less memory for the same items
optionB: It sorts the items automatically as they are added
optionC: It removes the possibility of reaching into the middle, so the invariant cannot be broken
optionD: Its operations are asymptotically faster than appending to and removing from an array
correctAnswerText: It removes the possibility of reaching into the middle, so the invariant cannot be broken
explanation: Both are constant time at the end, so speed is not the argument. The value is the restriction: code that cannot index into the middle cannot accidentally depend on doing so.

prompt: Rewriting a deep recursion to use an explicit stack trades away readability. What does it buy?
optionA: Control of the depth, so a large input fails gracefully rather than overflowing
optionB: Automatic parallel execution of the pending work
optionC: A lower asymptotic complexity, because the pending work is no longer duplicated
optionD: Freedom from needing a base case
correctAnswerText: Control of the depth, so a large input fails gracefully rather than overflowing
explanation: The work and its cost are the same; what changes is that the memory is yours to bound and inspect rather than the runtime's to exhaust.

prompt: A design uses a stack, but the code repeatedly pops items into a temporary list to find one, then pushes them all back. What does this indicate?
optionA: The items should be sorted before being pushed
optionB: The temporary list should be a stack as well
optionC: The stack implementation is inefficient and should be replaced
optionD: The access pattern is not last-in first-out, so the structure is wrong
correctAnswerText: The access pattern is not last-in first-out, so the structure is wrong
explanation: Fighting a structure to get at what it deliberately hides is the clearest sign it is the wrong one. Needing arbitrary lookup points at a map or a list.

prompt: A queue can be built from two stacks by pushing onto one and, when the other is empty, moving everything across. Why does moving everything produce the right order?
optionA: The two reversals cancel only because the counts are equal
optionB: The second stack sorts the items as they arrive
optionC: The move preserves the existing order, which was already first-in first-out throughout
optionD: Popping the first stack reverses it, and a reversed reversal is the arrival order
correctAnswerText: Popping the first stack reverses it, and a reversed reversal is the arrival order
explanation: One reversal turns last-in first-out into first-in first-out. The second stack then serves in arrival order until it empties and the transfer repeats.

prompt: In the two-stack queue, one dequeue occasionally moves every item across. What is the cost per operation overall?
optionA: Linear, because the expensive case can happen at any time
optionB: Constant on average, because each item is moved across exactly once
optionC: Logarithmic, because the transfers halve the work each time
optionD: Unpredictable, because it depends on the order of calls
correctAnswerText: Constant on average, because each item is moved across exactly once
explanation: An item is pushed once, moved once and popped once however many operations pass in between, so the total work is proportional to the items. Judging by the worst single call overstates it.

prompt: An undo stack in a long-running editor is given a maximum size. What is the reasoning?
optionA: A bounded stack performs its operations faster
optionB: The structure requires a capacity to be declared before anything can be pushed
optionC: Unbounded history would grow without limit, and old undo steps have little value
optionD: Undo cannot work correctly beyond a fixed depth
correctAnswerText: Unbounded history would grow without limit, and old undo steps have little value
explanation: It is a product decision about memory against usefulness, not a technical constraint. Discarding from the bottom is an addition the plain structure does not provide.

prompt: Validating that HTML tags are correctly nested needs a stack, but validating that a file has an even number of lines does not. What distinguishes them?
optionA: Counting lines is impossible without a structure to hold them
optionB: Nesting requires remembering what is still open and in what order
optionC: One problem is larger than the other
optionD: Tags are strings and lines are numbers
correctAnswerText: Nesting requires remembering what is still open and in what order
explanation: A counter suffices when only the total matters. Nesting needs the identity and order of what remains open, which is precisely what a stack holds.

prompt: For an expression containing only round brackets, a simple counter can replace the stack. Why does that stop working once several bracket types are allowed?
optionA: It does not stop working; a counter is always sufficient
optionB: A counter cannot represent numbers large enough
optionC: A counter records how many are open but not which kinds, so "([)]" passes
optionD: Several bracket types make the input longer than a counter can track
correctAnswerText: A counter records how many are open but not which kinds, so "([)]" passes
explanation: With one type, identity is implied. With several, the closer must match a specific opener, and only a structure that remembers order can say which.

prompt: Which of these problems is NOT naturally solved with a stack?
optionA: Finding the next greater element to the right of each item
optionB: Finding the two numbers in a list that sum to a target
optionC: Checking that brackets are balanced
optionD: Evaluating a postfix expression
correctAnswerText: Finding the two numbers in a list that sum to a target
explanation: Summing to a target wants a hash map for constant-time lookup of the complement. The other three all depend on the most recent unresolved item, which is stack-shaped.

prompt: Finding the next greater element for every item is solved in one pass with a stack. What is kept on it?
optionA: The greatest value found so far
optionB: The items already answered, so they can be reported at the end
optionC: Items still waiting for a greater value to appear
optionD: Every item seen so far, in arrival order
correctAnswerText: Items still waiting for a greater value to appear
explanation: An item stays until something larger arrives, which resolves it and pops it. Items already answered leave, which is why one pass suffices rather than a comparison against everything.

prompt: A queue removes items in which order relative to how they were added?
optionA: The first item added is removed first
optionB: Items are removed in an unpredictable order
optionC: The smallest item is removed first
optionD: The last item added is removed first
correctAnswerText: The first item added is removed first
explanation: A queue is first-in, first-out — the order people expect of anything described as a queue. Removing the last item added is stack behaviour.

prompt: Which operation adds an item to a queue?
optionA: dequeue
optionB: enqueue
optionC: peek
optionD: push
correctAnswerText: enqueue
explanation: enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front. push belongs to a stack, and peek only reads.

prompt: From which end does dequeue remove an item?
optionA: The back, where the newest item sits
optionB: Either end, whichever holds fewer items
optionC: The front, where the oldest item sits
optionD: The middle, to keep the queue balanced
correctAnswerText: The front, where the oldest item sits
explanation: Items enter at the back and leave at the front, which is what keeps the order fair. A structure removing from the back would be a stack.

prompt: At which end does enqueue add an item?
optionA: Wherever a gap has appeared
optionB: The front, ahead of everything already waiting
optionC: In sorted position among the waiting items
optionD: The back, behind everything already waiting
correctAnswerText: The back, behind everything already waiting
explanation: Joining at the back is what makes the wait fair. Adding at the front would let a late arrival be served first.

prompt: Which everyday system behaves like a queue?
optionA: A dictionary looked up by word
optionB: An editor undoing the most recent change first
optionC: A printer serving jobs in the order they were sent
optionD: A leaderboard ordered by score
correctAnswerText: A printer serving jobs in the order they were sent
explanation: Order of arrival decides order of service, which is first-in first-out. Undo is last-in first-out, and the other two are not about removal order at all.

prompt: What happens when dequeue is called on an empty queue?
optionA: It waits until an item arrives
optionB: It is an error condition the caller must handle
optionC: It returns the item most recently removed
optionD: It returns zero as a default value
correctAnswerText: It is an error condition the caller must handle
explanation: There is nothing to return, so the call cannot succeed. Some concurrent queues do block and wait, but a plain queue does not — the caller checks first.

prompt: Which item in a queue can be read without removing anything?
optionA: Any item, by its position
optionB: The one at the back
optionC: The one at the front
optionD: None — every read removes an item
correctAnswerText: The one at the front
explanation: A queue exposes the front for reading, as a stack exposes its top. Reaching the middle is not an operation it offers.

prompt: Why do operating systems use queues for tasks waiting to run?
optionA: So that the shortest task always runs first
optionB: So that waiting tasks are served in the order they arrived
optionC: So that tasks can be searched for by name
optionD: So that a task can be removed from the middle cheaply
correctAnswerText: So that waiting tasks are served in the order they arrived
explanation: A plain queue gives fairness by arrival. Serving the shortest first is a different policy and needs a different structure.

prompt: What does the size of a queue report?
optionA: How many items have been removed so far
optionB: How many items it has ever held
optionC: How many items are currently waiting
optionD: How many items it can hold before it is full
correctAnswerText: How many items are currently waiting
explanation: Size is the present count. Capacity and history are different quantities, and only some queue implementations track either.

prompt: A stack is last-in first-out. A queue is:
optionA: First-in first-out
optionB: Last-in last-out
optionC: Ordered by priority
optionD: Sorted on removal
correctAnswerText: First-in first-out
explanation: First-in first-out. "Last-in last-out" describes the same thing in a confusing way and is not the standard term; priority order is a different structure.

prompt: Starting from an empty queue: enqueue 3, enqueue 7, enqueue 9. What does dequeue return?
optionA: Nothing — the queue is empty
explanation: 3 arrived first, so it leaves first. Answering 9 is reading the structure as a stack.

prompt: Starting from an empty queue: enqueue 4, enqueue 8, dequeue, enqueue 2. What is at the front now?
optionC: The queue is empty
explanation: The dequeue removed 4, leaving 8 at the front. Enqueueing 2 puts it behind 8, so 8 is still first out.

prompt: The letters A, B, C are enqueued in that order, then all three are dequeued. In what order do they come out?
optionA: A, C, B
optionB: B, A, C
optionC: C, B, A
optionD: A, B, C
correctAnswerText: A, B, C
explanation: A queue preserves the order it received, which is exactly why it is used where fairness matters. Reversal is what a stack does.

prompt: enqueue 5, enqueue 6, dequeue, enqueue 7, dequeue, dequeue. What is the sequence of dequeued values?
explanation: Each dequeue takes the oldest remaining item, so arrival order is preserved whatever the interleaving of the operations.

prompt: A queue starts empty. Three enqueues and one dequeue are performed. How many items remain?
explanation: Each enqueue adds one and each dequeue removes one, so the net is two regardless of the values or the order of the calls.

prompt: The same items are added to a queue and to a stack, then everything is removed from each. How do the outputs compare?
optionA: It depends on how many items there were
optionB: The stack output is the reverse of the queue output
optionC: Both produce the same order
optionD: The queue output is sorted and the stack output is not
correctAnswerText: The stack output is the reverse of the queue output
explanation: A queue preserves order and a stack reverses it, so one output is always the reverse of the other whatever the items.

prompt: Support tickets must be answered in the order they were raised. Which structure fits?
optionA: A stack
optionB: A queue
optionC: A sorted list keyed on the customer name
optionD: A hash map keyed on the ticket id
correctAnswerText: A queue
explanation: Order of arrival deciding order of service is the definition of a queue. A stack would answer the newest ticket first, which is the opposite of what was asked.

prompt: A queue holds four items and the front is read twice without dequeuing. How many items does it hold?
explanation: Reading the front does not remove it, so the size is unchanged however many times it is read.

prompt: To find whether a particular value is waiting somewhere in a queue, you must:
optionA: Jump to its position using an index
optionB: Sort the queue and then search it
optionC: Dequeue items until you find it, and re-enqueue what you removed
optionD: Look it up directly by its value
correctAnswerText: Dequeue items until you find it, and re-enqueue what you removed
explanation: Only the front is reachable, so getting at the middle means removing what is ahead of it. Needing to search is a sign the structure is wrong for the job.

prompt: How does a priority queue differ from a plain queue?
optionA: It keeps its items permanently sorted by arrival time
optionB: It allows items to be removed from either end
optionC: It serves the highest-priority item next rather than the oldest
optionD: It holds more items before it becomes full
correctAnswerText: It serves the highest-priority item next rather than the oldest
explanation: Priority replaces arrival order as the rule for what leaves next, which means a newly added urgent item can overtake items that have waited longer.

prompt: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level. Which structure holds the nodes still to visit?
optionA: A stack, so the most recently found node is visited next
optionB: A hash map, keyed by node
optionC: A queue, so nearer nodes are visited before further ones
optionD: A sorted list, ordered by node name
correctAnswerText: A queue, so nearer nodes are visited before further ones
explanation: Nodes discovered earlier are nearer, and a queue serves them first — which is what produces the level-by-level order. Using a stack instead gives depth-first search.

prompt: Work arrives faster than it can be processed, and must not be lost. What does putting a queue between the two parts achieve?
optionA: It discards the oldest work to keep up
optionB: It absorbs the bursts, letting the consumer work at its own pace
optionC: It makes the consumer process each item faster
optionD: It guarantees the work is processed in priority order
correctAnswerText: It absorbs the bursts, letting the consumer work at its own pace
explanation: A queue decouples the rates: the producer is not blocked by a slow consumer, and nothing is lost while the backlog drains. It changes nothing about processing speed.

prompt: A queue is built on an array, removing from index 0 each time. What is the cost of each dequeue?
optionA: Logarithmic, because the array is halved
optionB: Linear, because every remaining item shifts down one place
optionC: Constant, but only while the queue is short
optionD: Constant, because only one item is removed
correctAnswerText: Linear, because every remaining item shifts down one place
explanation: Removing the first element of an array moves every other element. It is the classic reason a naive array queue is slow, and why real ones use two indices or a linked list.

prompt: A circular buffer implements a queue on a fixed array. What makes it circular?
optionA: The items are physically rotated after every removal
optionB: The front and back indices wrap to the start when they pass the end
optionC: The array grows and shrinks as items arrive and leave
optionD: It stores the items in reverse order once it is half full
correctAnswerText: The front and back indices wrap to the start when they pass the end
explanation: Wrapping the indices reuses the space freed at the start without moving anything, which is what makes both operations constant time on a fixed array.

prompt: A queue built on a linked list keeps references to both the head and the tail. Why the tail?
optionA: So the list can be sorted more cheaply
optionB: So enqueue can add at the end without walking the whole list
optionC: So the list can be traversed backwards when searching
optionD: So the size can be calculated without counting
correctAnswerText: So enqueue can add at the end without walking the whole list
explanation: Without a tail reference, reaching the end means following every link, making enqueue linear. Keeping both references makes both operations constant time.

prompt: Requests to a rate-limited API are queued rather than sent immediately. What does this achieve?
optionA: The API raises its limit for a queued caller
optionB: Each request completes faster than it would alone
optionC: The sending rate is controlled while the order of requests is kept
optionD: Failed requests are automatically retried
correctAnswerText: The sending rate is controlled while the order of requests is kept
explanation: The queue turns an uncontrolled burst into a paced stream without losing anything or reordering it. Retrying is separate behaviour the queue does not provide by itself.

prompt: On an unweighted graph, why does breadth-first search find the shortest path?
optionA: It compares the length of every possible path before choosing
optionB: Every node one step away is visited before any node two steps away
optionC: It always follows the lowest-numbered neighbour first
optionD: It revisits nodes until no shorter route can be found
correctAnswerText: Every node one step away is visited before any node two steps away
explanation: Because the queue serves nearer nodes first, the first time a node is reached is by the fewest steps. No path comparison is needed, which is why it is so cheap.

prompt: What does a double-ended queue allow that a plain queue does not?
optionA: Removing items from the middle by value
optionB: Automatic ordering of its items by priority
optionC: Holding two separate sequences at once
optionD: Adding and removing at both ends
correctAnswerText: Adding and removing at both ends
explanation: A deque generalises both a queue and a stack, since either behaviour can be had by using one end or both. It still offers nothing for reaching the middle.

prompt: What is the cost of enqueue and dequeue on a well-implemented queue?
optionA: Constant time for both, because only the ends are touched
optionB: Linear time for dequeue and constant for enqueue
optionC: Logarithmic for both, because order must be maintained
optionD: It depends on how many items are waiting
correctAnswerText: Constant time for both, because only the ends are touched
explanation: Neither operation inspects the items in between. A linear dequeue is the signature of a naive array implementation, not of the structure itself.

prompt: Printing a tree one level at a time uses a queue. What is enqueued as each node is processed?
optionA: Only the node's leftmost child, to keep the queue from growing too fast
optionB: That node itself again, so it can be revisited later
optionC: The node's parent, so the level can be reconstructed
optionD: That node's children, so they are processed after the rest of this level
correctAnswerText: That node's children, so they are processed after the rest of this level
explanation: Children join the back and so wait behind everything already on the current level. That is exactly what produces level-by-level output.

prompt: A support queue keeps answering the newest ticket first. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: Items are being removed from the same end they are added to
optionB: The queue has exceeded its capacity and is discarding items
optionC: The tickets are being sorted by their identifier
optionD: Two consumers are competing for the same ticket
correctAnswerText: Items are being removed from the same end they are added to
explanation: Adding and removing at one end is stack behaviour, which serves newest first. The symptom names the defect precisely.

prompt: A queue is fast with a hundred items and noticeably slow with a hundred thousand, though each item is the same size. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The items are being compared to each other every time one is inserted
optionB: Dequeue removes from the front of an array, shifting everything each time
optionC: The consumer has become slower as the backlog grew
optionD: The queue is running out of memory and swapping
correctAnswerText: Dequeue removes from the front of an array, shifting everything each time
explanation: Cost rising with the number waiting points at work proportional to the size — the shift. A correctly built queue is indifferent to how many items it holds.

prompt: Work is enqueued faster than it is dequeued, indefinitely. What happens?
optionA: The queue grows without limit until memory runs out
optionB: The queue automatically drops its oldest items
optionC: Enqueue starts to fail once a default limit is reached
optionD: The producer is automatically slowed to match
correctAnswerText: The queue grows without limit until memory runs out
explanation: A plain queue has no policy for a permanent imbalance — it simply holds everything. Dropping, refusing or applying back pressure are choices somebody has to add.

prompt: In a circular buffer, front and back indices being equal is ambiguous. Why?
optionA: It means the array was allocated with the wrong size
optionB: It happens only when the indices have wrapped an odd number of times
optionC: It happens both when the buffer is empty and when it is completely full
optionD: It happens whenever an item is removed from the middle
correctAnswerText: It happens both when the buffer is empty and when it is completely full
explanation: Both states leave the indices in the same place, so implementations keep a count or deliberately leave one slot unused to tell them apart.

prompt: A linked-list queue empties correctly but then enqueueing again appears to lose items. What is the likely error?
optionA: The list is being traversed from the wrong end
optionB: The head reference is being updated twice on every removal, so one node gets skipped
optionC: The tail reference was not cleared when the queue emptied, so it points at a removed node
optionD: The nodes are being freed before they are dequeued
correctAnswerText: The tail reference was not cleared when the queue emptied, so it points at a removed node
explanation: Emptying must reset both references. A tail still pointing at a detached node means new items are attached to something no longer reachable from the head.

prompt: A breadth-first search on a graph with cycles never terminates. What is missing?
optionA: A record of which nodes have already been seen
optionB: A check that the graph is connected
optionC: A limit on how deep the search may go
optionD: A second queue for the next level
correctAnswerText: A record of which nodes have already been seen
explanation: Without it, a cycle re-enqueues nodes already visited and the queue never empties. A depth limit would hide the symptom rather than fix the cause.

prompt: Two workers read from one queue and occasionally process the same item twice. What is the cause?
optionA: The queue duplicates its items whenever more than one worker attaches to it at the same time
optionB: Reading the front and removing it are separate steps, and both workers read before either removed
optionC: The workers are processing at different speeds
optionD: The queue is returning items in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: Reading the front and removing it are separate steps, and both workers read before either removed
explanation: A read-then-remove pair is not atomic, so a gap between them lets two workers claim one item — the same read-then-write race that causes double selling of stock.

prompt: A priority queue is used for support tickets, and some low-priority tickets are never answered. Why?
optionA: The queue has lost the low-priority items
optionB: The queue can only hold a fixed number of priorities
optionC: Low-priority items expire automatically after a time
optionD: Higher-priority tickets keep arriving and always overtake them
correctAnswerText: Higher-priority tickets keep arriving and always overtake them
explanation: This is starvation, and it is inherent to strict priority rather than a defect. Systems that care about it raise an item's priority as it waits.

prompt: A function looks for a value by dequeuing until it finds it, then returns. What has it done to the queue?
optionA: Reversed the order of the remaining items
optionB: Removed everything ahead of the match, and the match itself
optionC: Moved the removed items to the back, preserving their order
optionD: Left the queue exactly as it was
correctAnswerText: Removed everything ahead of the match, and the match itself
explanation: Dequeued items are gone unless the code deliberately re-enqueues them. A search that empties what it searched is a defect hidden inside a function that looks correct.

prompt: A loop dequeues until the queue is empty, and processing each item enqueues another. What is the risk?
optionA: The loop ends early, leaving the new items unprocessed
optionB: Items added during the loop are silently discarded
optionC: The loop may never end, because the queue is refilled as fast as it drains
optionD: The queue will reorder itself and items will be processed twice
correctAnswerText: The loop may never end, because the queue is refilled as fast as it drains
explanation: This is exactly how breadth-first search works, and it terminates only because nodes stop being new. Without something that bounds the additions, it does not.

prompt: What single question best decides between a queue and a stack for a problem?
optionA: Should the oldest waiting item be handled next, or the newest?
optionB: Will items need to be searched for by value?
optionC: Is the number of items known in advance?
optionD: Which structure is faster for the expected number of items?
correctAnswerText: Should the oldest waiting item be handled next, or the newest?
explanation: The two differ only in which end is served, so the ordering requirement settles it. Their costs are the same, and neither supports searching.

prompt: A queue between two services is given a maximum size. What must be decided alongside it?
optionA: Which items are allowed to be added to it
optionB: What happens when it is full — refuse, drop, or make the producer wait
optionC: How often the queue should be emptied by a scheduled background job
optionD: Whether the consumer should read from the back instead
correctAnswerText: What happens when it is full — refuse, drop, or make the producer wait
explanation: A limit without a policy just moves the failure. Refusing, discarding and applying back pressure are three different promises to whoever produces the work.

prompt: Moving from a plain queue to a priority queue for support tickets trades away what?
optionA: The ability to hold more than a fixed number of tickets
optionB: The guarantee that waiting long enough means being served
optionC: Constant-time addition of new tickets
optionD: The ability to inspect the next ticket before handling it
correctAnswerText: The guarantee that waiting long enough means being served
explanation: Strict priority allows indefinite starvation, which a plain queue cannot produce. That is the real cost, and it is a policy decision rather than a technical one.

prompt: For a queue that will hold millions of items, why is a plain array with removal from index 0 the wrong choice?
optionA: Every removal moves every remaining item, so the total work grows with the square of the count
optionB: The items would be returned in the wrong order
optionC: An array cannot hold that many items at all
optionD: Arrays cannot be resized once they have been created, so the queue would very soon fill up
correctAnswerText: Every removal moves every remaining item, so the total work grows with the square of the count
explanation: Each dequeue is linear, so draining the whole queue is quadratic. A circular buffer or a linked list makes the same work linear overall.

prompt: Searching a very deep graph for a node known to be near the start, why prefer breadth-first over depth-first?
optionA: It is the only one of the two that detects cycles
optionB: It finds near nodes first, rather than descending a long branch away from the target
optionC: It examines each node fewer times
optionD: It uses less memory than depth-first search on any graph, whatever its shape
correctAnswerText: It finds near nodes first, rather than descending a long branch away from the target
explanation: Depth-first commits to one branch and may explore a great deal before returning. On a wide graph breadth-first uses more memory, not less — the choice is about where the answer is.

prompt: Two services are separated by a message queue. What does this buy that a direct call does not?
optionA: The work is completed faster than calling directly
optionB: The receiver is guaranteed to process every message exactly once
optionC: Neither service needs error handling any longer
optionD: The sender succeeds even while the receiver is down or slow
correctAnswerText: The sender succeeds even while the receiver is down or slow
explanation: The queue holds the work until the receiver is ready, which is availability rather than speed. Exactly-once delivery is famously hard and is not something a queue simply provides.

prompt: Code repeatedly dequeues items into a list to find one, then re-enqueues them all. What does that indicate?
optionA: The items should be sorted before being enqueued
optionB: The queue implementation should be replaced with a faster one
optionC: The list should be replaced with a second queue
optionD: The access pattern is not first-in first-out, so the structure is wrong
correctAnswerText: The access pattern is not first-in first-out, so the structure is wrong
explanation: Fighting a structure to reach what it deliberately hides is the clearest sign it is the wrong one. Arbitrary lookup wants a map, not a queue.

prompt: A queue can be built from two stacks. What makes this work?
optionA: Moving items from one stack to the other reverses them, turning newest-first into oldest-first
optionB: Each stack holds half the items, so neither ever reverses
optionC: The second stack keeps the items permanently sorted by arrival
optionD: One stack holds all of the odd-numbered items and the other holds the even-numbered ones
correctAnswerText: Moving items from one stack to the other reverses them, turning newest-first into oldest-first
explanation: A single reversal converts last-in first-out into first-in first-out. The second stack then serves in arrival order until it empties and the transfer repeats.

prompt: Which problem is NOT naturally solved with a queue?
optionA: Processing print jobs in the order they were submitted
optionB: Printing a tree one level at a time
optionC: Finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph
optionD: Checking that brackets in an expression are correctly nested
correctAnswerText: Checking that brackets in an expression are correctly nested
explanation: Nesting depends on the most recently opened item, which is stack-shaped. The other three all depend on the oldest waiting item.

prompt: Finding the maximum of every window of fixed width across a list uses a double-ended queue. Why are items removed from the back as well as the front?
optionA: The front drops items outside the window; the back drops ones a larger value made useless
optionB: Removing from both ends is what keeps the deque sorted automatically as items arrive
optionC: The back holds the window and the front holds the answers
optionD: The back is used only when the front becomes full
correctAnswerText: The front drops items outside the window; the back drops ones a larger value made useless
explanation: A smaller value with a larger one after it can never be a maximum again, so it is discarded on arrival. That is what keeps the deque small and the whole pass linear.

prompt: What does a node in a singly linked list hold?
optionA: A value and a reference to the next node
optionB: A value and its position in the list
optionC: A value and references to both neighbours
optionD: A value only, with order kept elsewhere
correctAnswerText: A value and a reference to the next node
explanation: Value plus a link to the next node. Holding both neighbours makes it a doubly linked list, and no node stores its own position — that is what an array index does.

prompt: What is the head of a linked list?
optionA: The node most recently added to the list
optionB: The node holding the largest value
optionC: A count of how many nodes the list holds
optionD: A reference to the first node, and the only way into the list
correctAnswerText: A reference to the first node, and the only way into the list
explanation: The head is the entry point. Lose it and the whole list becomes unreachable, however many nodes still exist in memory.

prompt: What does the last node of a singly linked list point to?
optionA: To the node before it
optionB: To itself, to mark the end
optionC: Nothing — its next reference is null
optionD: Back to the head of the list
correctAnswerText: Nothing — its next reference is null
explanation: A null next marks the end. Pointing back to the head would make it a circular list, which is a deliberate variant rather than the default.

prompt: How do you reach the fifth item of a linked list?
optionA: Follow the links from the head, four times
optionB: Read it directly at index four
optionC: Jump to it using the list's position table
optionD: Search the list for the value you want
correctAnswerText: Follow the links from the head, four times
explanation: There is no index and no position table. Reaching any node means walking there from the head, which is the central cost of the structure.

prompt: How are the nodes of a linked list arranged in memory?
optionA: Side by side in one continuous block
optionB: In sorted order by their values
optionC: In the order the memory was allocated, with no gaps
optionD: Anywhere — each node points at the next wherever it happens to be
correctAnswerText: Anywhere — each node points at the next wherever it happens to be
explanation: Nodes are allocated independently and joined by references. A continuous block is what an array is, and it is the reason an array can index and a list cannot.

prompt: What distinguishes a doubly linked list?
optionA: It keeps two separate chains of the same nodes
optionB: It stores two values in every node
optionC: It has both a head and a tail reference
optionD: Each node also holds a reference to the previous node
correctAnswerText: Each node also holds a reference to the previous node
explanation: Each node links both ways, which is what allows backwards traversal and removal without finding the predecessor first. A tail reference is useful but not what makes a list doubly linked.

prompt: How does a linked list grow?
optionA: It doubles its capacity once it is full
optionB: Its block of memory is resized when it fills
optionC: One node is allocated at a time, as it is needed
optionD: Its size is fixed when the list is created
correctAnswerText: One node is allocated at a time, as it is needed
explanation: There is no block and no capacity, so nothing is ever resized or copied. Doubling is how a dynamic array grows, which is a different structure.

prompt: In a singly linked list, can you move from a node back to the one before it?
optionA: Yes, by following the next reference backwards
optionB: Yes, every node keeps its predecessor
optionC: Only if the list has a tail reference
optionD: No — the links only point forwards
correctAnswerText: No — the links only point forwards
explanation: A reference points one way only. Going back means starting again from the head, which is why some algorithms keep a trailing reference as they walk.

prompt: What is the cost of adding a node at the front of a linked list?
optionA: Constant — the new node points at the old head, and the head is updated
optionB: It depends on how many nodes the list already holds
optionC: Linear — the list must be walked to find the end first
optionD: Linear — every existing node must be moved along one place
correctAnswerText: Constant — the new node points at the old head, and the head is updated
explanation: Two references change and nothing else is touched. This is the operation linked lists are genuinely good at, and it is why they back stacks and queues.

prompt: What makes a linked list circular?
optionA: Its nodes are visited in rotating order
optionB: The last node points back to the first instead of to null
optionC: The nodes are physically arranged in a ring in memory
optionD: It can be traversed in either direction
correctAnswerText: The last node points back to the first instead of to null
explanation: One reference changes and the list has no end, which suits round-robin scheduling. It also means a traversal with no stopping rule never terminates.

prompt: A list is empty. Three values are each added at the front, in the order 1, 2, 3. Reading from the head, what is the order?
explanation: Each new node becomes the head, so the last added is read first. Adding at the front reverses the insertion order, which is why it underlies a stack.

prompt: A list holds A → B → C. B is removed. What must change?
optionA: The head must be moved to C
optionB: C's next reference must point at A
optionC: A's next reference must point at C
optionD: Nothing — removing B breaks the links automatically
correctAnswerText: A's next reference must point at C
explanation: The chain is repaired by pointing the predecessor at the successor. Nothing happens automatically; a node simply removed leaves the list broken at that point.

prompt: Reading the thousandth item costs what, in an array and in a linked list?
optionA: Constant in both
optionB: Linear in the array, constant in the list
optionC: Constant in the array, linear in the list
optionD: Linear in both
correctAnswerText: Constant in the array, linear in the list
explanation: An array computes the address arithmetically; a list must follow a thousand references. This single difference decides most choices between them.

prompt: How is the length of a linked list found, if no count is kept?
optionA: By subtracting the head address from the tail address
optionB: By asking the last node for its position
optionC: By walking from the head to the end, counting nodes
optionD: By reading a length stored on the head node
correctAnswerText: By walking from the head to the end, counting nodes
explanation: Nothing knows the length, so it must be counted — a linear operation. Implementations that need it cheaply maintain a counter as nodes are added and removed.

prompt: Adding to the end of a singly linked list with only a head reference costs:
optionA: Logarithmic time, because the list is halved
optionB: Linear time, because the end must be found first
optionC: Constant time, because only one link changes
optionD: Constant time, because the last node is always known
correctAnswerText: Linear time, because the end must be found first
explanation: Only one link changes, but getting to it means walking the whole list. Keeping a tail reference is what makes appending constant.

prompt: Why does a linked list use more memory than an array holding the same values?
optionA: It always allocates twice the space it needs
optionB: Every node stores a copy of the value before it
optionC: Every node stores a reference alongside its value
optionD: It keeps a position number on every node
correctAnswerText: Every node stores a reference alongside its value
explanation: The link is the overhead, and it is per node. For small values such as single bytes, the reference can cost more than the data itself.

prompt: Finding whether a value is present in a sorted linked list costs:
optionA: Linear time, because binary search needs index access
optionB: Constant time, because sorting allows direct lookup
optionC: Logarithmic time, because the list is sorted
optionD: Logarithmic time, but only for a doubly linked list
correctAnswerText: Linear time, because binary search needs index access
explanation: Binary search must jump to the middle, and a list has no way to. Sorting a linked list buys early termination but not the logarithmic search an array gets.

prompt: You already hold a reference to a node. Inserting a new node directly after it costs:
optionA: It depends on how far the node is from the head
optionB: Linear time — the list must be walked from the head
optionC: Linear time — the following nodes shift along
optionD: Constant time — two references are updated
correctAnswerText: Constant time — two references are updated
explanation: Holding the node is the expensive part, and this question grants it. This is the case that makes "insertion is O(1)" true, and it is narrower than it sounds.

prompt: Inserting into the middle of an array costs linear time. Why?
optionA: The index of every element is recalculated and stored
optionB: The array must be sorted again after the insertion
optionC: A new array is always allocated for each insertion
optionD: Every element after the insertion point shifts along one place
correctAnswerText: Every element after the insertion point shifts along one place
explanation: Contiguous storage means making room physically moves things. Indices are computed rather than stored, so nothing needs recalculating.

prompt: Given a reference to a node, why is removal easier in a doubly linked list?
optionA: The node can delete itself without any of the references changing
optionB: The list automatically reorders itself after a removal
optionC: Removal is constant in both, so it is not easier
optionD: The node knows its predecessor, so the chain can be repaired immediately
correctAnswerText: The node knows its predecessor, so the chain can be repaired immediately
explanation: In a singly linked list the predecessor must be found by walking from the head, making removal linear despite holding the node. The backward link removes that walk.

prompt: Reversing a singly linked list in place works by:
optionA: Walking the list and pointing each node at the one before it
optionB: Following the previous references from the tail
optionC: Building a new list and copying the values in backwards
optionD: Swapping the values held in the first and last nodes, then moving inwards
correctAnswerText: Walking the list and pointing each node at the one before it
explanation: The links are redirected as the walk proceeds, which needs three references — previous, current and next. Swapping inwards needs backward movement a singly linked list has not got.

prompt: While reversing a list, why must the next node be saved before the current link is changed?
optionA: Without it the loop cannot tell how long the list is
optionB: Redirecting the link destroys the only route to the rest of the list
optionC: The next node must be counted before it can be visited properly
optionD: The saved reference is what the new head is taken from
correctAnswerText: Redirecting the link destroys the only route to the rest of the list
explanation: Once current.next points backwards, the remainder is unreachable. Forgetting the temporary reference is the single commonest bug in this algorithm.

prompt: Finding the middle node in one pass uses two references moving at different speeds. Why does it work?
optionA: When the faster one reaches the end, the slower has covered half the distance
optionB: The slower one stops once the faster one has doubled back
optionC: The two meet in the middle because they start from opposite ends of the list
optionD: The faster one counts the nodes while the slower one waits
correctAnswerText: When the faster one reaches the end, the slower has covered half the distance
explanation: Moving one node while the other moves two puts the slow reference at half the distance when the fast one finishes. It avoids the two passes counting would need.

prompt: The same two-speed technique detects a cycle. What indicates one is present?
optionA: The faster reference catches up and meets the slower one
optionB: Both references return to the head together
optionC: The faster reference reaches a null next reference
optionD: The slower reference visits a node twice
correctAnswerText: The faster reference catches up and meets the slower one
explanation: Inside a loop the gap closes by one each step, so they must meet. Reaching null proves the opposite — that the list ends and has no cycle.

prompt: Many list implementations keep a dummy node before the first real one. What does it buy?
optionA: It prevents the head reference from ever being lost
optionB: It allows the list to be traversed backwards
optionC: It records how many nodes the list holds
optionD: Insertion and removal at the front stop being special cases
correctAnswerText: Insertion and removal at the front stop being special cases
explanation: With a node always in front, every insertion has a predecessor and one code path handles them all. It is a readability and correctness device rather than a performance one.

prompt: A stack is implemented on a singly linked list. Which end should be the top?
optionA: Either — both ends cost the same on a linked list
optionB: The middle, so neither end becomes a bottleneck
optionC: The tail, because that is where new items naturally belong
optionD: The head, because adding and removing there are constant time
correctAnswerText: The head, because adding and removing there are constant time
explanation: Without a tail reference the end is linear to reach, and even with one, removing from the end of a singly linked list is linear. The head is constant for both.

prompt: Finding the nth node from the end in a single pass uses two references. How?
optionA: Both start at the head and one moves at twice the speed
optionB: One walks forwards from the head and the other backwards from the tail
optionC: One counts the nodes and the other divides the total by n
optionD: One starts n nodes ahead; when it reaches the end the other is at the answer
correctAnswerText: One starts n nodes ahead; when it reaches the end the other is at the answer
explanation: A fixed gap of n is maintained, so the trailing reference lands exactly n from the end. The two-speed technique answers a different question — the middle.

prompt: An LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list. What does each contribute?
optionA: The map keeps the order and the list stores the values
optionB: The map finds an entry instantly; the list keeps the order and allows cheap removal
optionC: The map holds recent entries and the list holds older ones
optionD: The list finds the entries and the map records how often each one is used
correctAnswerText: The map finds an entry instantly; the list keeps the order and allows cheap removal
explanation: Neither structure alone does both: a map has no order, and a list cannot look up. Combining them is what makes every operation constant time.

prompt: Merging two sorted linked lists into one sorted list works by:
optionA: Comparing the two front nodes and taking the smaller each time
optionB: Appending the second list and sorting the result
optionC: Inserting each node of the second into its place in the first
optionD: Counting both lists and allocating a new one of that size
correctAnswerText: Comparing the two front nodes and taking the smaller each time
explanation: Each step takes the smaller of the two heads, which is linear overall. Merging by relinking also needs no extra memory, which is why merge sort suits linked lists.

prompt: A queue on a singly linked list keeps head and tail references. Which end serves which operation?
optionA: Remove at the tail, add at the head
optionB: Remove at the head, add at the tail
optionC: Both at the head, using the tail only for counting
optionD: Both at the tail, using the head only as an entry point
correctAnswerText: Remove at the head, add at the tail
explanation: Removing at the tail would need the predecessor, which is linear to find in a singly linked list. Head-out and tail-in keeps both operations constant.

prompt: A function walks a list by advancing the head reference itself. What happens afterwards?
optionA: Nothing at all, because head is restored automatically when the function returns
optionB: The walk fails immediately on the first node
optionC: The caller has lost the list, because head now points somewhere in the middle
optionD: The list is reversed as a side effect of the walk
correctAnswerText: The caller has lost the list, because head now points somewhere in the middle
explanation: Everything before the new head becomes unreachable. Traversal must use a separate reference, which is why a local variable is initialised from the head rather than used directly.

prompt: Code removes a node by setting its own next reference to null. What is the result?
optionA: The list is truncated at that node, because its predecessor still points at it
optionB: The predecessor is also removed from the list
optionC: The node is removed correctly and the chain then repairs itself automatically
optionD: The list becomes circular at that point
correctAnswerText: The list is truncated at that node, because its predecessor still points at it
explanation: Removal is done by the predecessor, not by the node itself. Clearing your own link severs everything after you while leaving you in place.

prompt: A traversal that should end never terminates, and the list was recently modified. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The list grew larger than the traversal expected
optionB: The head reference was not initialised before the walk
optionC: A link was set so that some node points back to an earlier one
optionD: The final node was removed, leaving no null link
correctAnswerText: A link was set so that some node points back to an earlier one
explanation: A cycle makes the walk loop forever. Removing the last node would leave its predecessor pointing at null, which ends the walk rather than extending it.

prompt: After reversing a list, only one node remains reachable from the head. What went wrong?
optionA: The head was not updated to the last node visited, so it still points at the old first node
optionB: The list contained a cycle before it was reversed
optionC: The loop ran one iteration too few, leaving the final node completely unlinked
optionD: The values were swapped rather than the links redirected
correctAnswerText: The head was not updated to the last node visited, so it still points at the old first node
explanation: The old first node is now the end, and its next is null — so from there the list appears to hold one item. Reversal must finish by moving the head.

prompt: A list keeps a tail reference. Nodes are removed from the end but the tail is not updated. What follows?
optionA: Traversal from the head stops one node early
optionB: Nothing at all, because the tail is recalculated on the very next append
optionC: The next append attaches to a node no longer in the list, and the item is lost
optionD: The list reports a length one greater than it holds
correctAnswerText: The next append attaches to a node no longer in the list, and the item is lost
explanation: A cached reference must be maintained by every operation that could invalidate it. Traversal from the head still works, which is what makes this so hard to spot.

prompt: Code meant to insert before a given node keeps inserting after it instead. What is the underlying difficulty?
optionA: The new node must be allocated before its position is known to the list
optionB: A singly linked list can only reach the predecessor by walking from the head
optionC: The head reference cannot be changed once the list exists
optionD: Inserting before a node is forbidden by the structure
correctAnswerText: A singly linked list can only reach the predecessor by walking from the head
explanation: Inserting before requires changing the predecessor's link, and the node does not know it. The usual workaround inserts after and swaps the values.

prompt: A loop reads a linked list using get(i) for i from 0 to n. Why is it unexpectedly slow?
optionA: Each get allocates a new node before returning the value
optionB: Each get walks from the head, making the whole loop quadratic
optionC: The list is re-sorted between successive calls
optionD: The loop reads every node twice, once forwards and once back
correctAnswerText: Each get walks from the head, making the whole loop quadratic
explanation: An interface that looks like an array hides a linear cost per call. Iterating with a single advancing reference makes the same loop linear.

prompt: A list function works on every test except an empty list, where it fails. What is the likely cause?
optionA: It allocates a node before checking the list length
optionB: It counts the nodes before deciding what to do
optionC: It reads head.next without first checking that head exists
optionD: It assumes the list has a tail reference
correctAnswerText: It reads head.next without first checking that head exists
explanation: An empty list has a null head, so any dereference fails immediately. The empty case and the single-node case are the two every list function must be tested against.

prompt: Two lists were built from the same nodes. Modifying one changes the other. Why?
optionA: Both hold references to the same node objects, not copies of them
optionB: The lists share a single head reference between them
optionC: Linked lists always synchronise nodes holding equal values
optionD: The second list was never fully built and reads from the first
correctAnswerText: Both hold references to the same node objects, not copies of them
explanation: Copying a list means allocating new nodes; copying references shares the nodes themselves. This is the same aliasing problem as a shallow copy of any object.

prompt: Traversing a circular list with a loop that stops on null never ends. What is the correct stopping rule?
optionA: Stop after visiting a fixed number of nodes
optionB: Stop when the next reference equals the current node
optionC: Stop on returning to the node the traversal started from
optionD: Stop when a node's value repeats
correctAnswerText: Stop on returning to the node the traversal started from
explanation: A circular list has no null, so the start node is the only reliable marker. A repeated value proves nothing — a list may legitimately hold duplicates.

prompt: "Insertion into a linked list is O(1)." What does this claim quietly assume?
optionA: That the insertion happens at the end rather than the middle
optionB: That the list has fewer items than an array would
optionC: That the list is kept sorted as items are added
optionD: That you already hold a reference to the node you are inserting beside
correctAnswerText: That you already hold a reference to the node you are inserting beside
explanation: Finding the position is linear, and it usually dominates. Quoted without that condition, the claim leads people to choose a list for a job an array does better.

prompt: Arrays often beat linked lists in practice even where the complexity suggests otherwise. Why?
optionA: Arrays are stored in compressed form and so occupy far less memory overall
optionB: Array elements sit together in memory, so reading one brings its neighbours into cache
optionC: Arrays use a faster instruction for reading a value
optionD: Linked lists must check for cycles on every traversal
correctAnswerText: Array elements sit together in memory, so reading one brings its neighbours into cache
explanation: Complexity counts operations and ignores their cost. Following scattered references defeats the cache, which is why measurement often contradicts the table.

prompt: Which requirement most genuinely favours a linked list over a dynamic array?
optionA: Frequent reads of items at arbitrary positions
optionB: Sorting the collection repeatedly
optionC: Storing a very large number of small values as compactly as possible
optionD: Constant-time removal while already holding a reference to the node
correctAnswerText: Constant-time removal while already holding a reference to the node
explanation: Holding the node is what makes the list win, which is why an LRU cache pairs one with a map. The other three are all cases where an array is better.

prompt: Why can an LRU cache not be built from a hash map alone?
optionA: A map has no way to store the time at which each entry was last used
optionB: A map has no order, so the least recently used entry cannot be identified
optionC: Map lookups become slower as entries are evicted
optionD: A map cannot hold enough entries for a cache
correctAnswerText: A map has no order, so the least recently used entry cannot be identified
explanation: It could store timestamps, but finding the oldest would then mean scanning everything. The list keeps that answer permanently at one end.

prompt: Choosing a doubly linked list over a singly linked one costs what?
optionA: Constant-time insertion at the head
optionB: The ability to use the list as a queue
optionC: The ability to traverse the whole list in the forward direction
optionD: An extra reference per node, and a second link to keep correct on every change
correctAnswerText: An extra reference per node, and a second link to keep correct on every change
explanation: Memory and, more importantly, correctness: every operation now maintains two links, and a missed one corrupts the list in a direction nobody tests.

prompt: Linked lists are taught heavily but used rarely in application code. What is the best justification for learning them?
optionA: They are the basis of trees, graphs and every structure built from linked nodes
optionB: They are simpler to implement correctly than an array
optionC: They are the structure most often required in real production projects
optionD: They outperform arrays in most production workloads
correctAnswerText: They are the basis of trees, graphs and every structure built from linked nodes
explanation: A tree is a node with several links and a graph is the general case. Understanding references and traversal here is what makes those tractable later.

prompt: In a memory-constrained system, what advantage does a linked list keep over a dynamic array?
optionA: It can be written to disk without being serialised
optionB: It never needs to allocate any further memory after it is created
optionC: It needs no single contiguous block, so it can use fragmented free space
optionD: It uses less memory per item stored
correctAnswerText: It needs no single contiguous block, so it can use fragmented free space
explanation: A growing array needs one unbroken block and must copy when it moves. A list allocates node by node, which can succeed where a large contiguous request fails.

prompt: Why is merge sort the usual choice for sorting a linked list, where quicksort suits an array?
optionA: Quicksort cannot be implemented on a linked list at all
optionB: Merge sort has a lower asymptotic complexity than quicksort in every case
optionC: Merging relinks nodes without random access or extra memory, which lists cannot afford
optionD: Merge sort keeps the list sorted as new nodes are added
correctAnswerText: Merging relinks nodes without random access or extra memory, which lists cannot afford
explanation: Quicksort depends on reaching arbitrary positions to partition, which is linear on a list. Merge sort only ever looks at the fronts, which a list gives cheaply.

prompt: The two-reference technique used on linked lists transfers to which other problem?
optionA: Finding a pair summing to a target in a sorted array, using two ends moving inwards
optionB: Counting how many distinct values appear in an unsorted collection
optionC: Looking up a value in a hash map by its key
optionD: Sorting a collection of integers in linear time
correctAnswerText: Finding a pair summing to a target in a sorted array, using two ends moving inwards
